organization.name: The Civic Vigilance
organization.entry:
The Civic Vigilance is {{FOGPORT_LINK}}’s constabulary, charged with preserving public order, investigating serious crimes, hunting dangerous creatures, and protecting the city from cults, riots, and unnatural threats. Its officers are formally addressed as constables, though most citizens call them Blackcoat Constables, Blackcoats, or simply the Coats.

Blackcoats are not beloved. They are feared, frequently corrupt, and notoriously heavy-handed—but Fogport is a city where an ordinary domestic disturbance may involve a ghoul in the chimney or a husband who has been dead for three weeks. Even their harshest critics become anxious when the Blackcoats stop patrolling their street.

Uniform and Equipment

A Blackcoat wears a long, tar-black greatcoat over a canvas-and-chain vest. A blackened steel gorget protects the throat, while steel bracers, heavy gloves, hobnailed boots, and a reinforced leather helmet offer some defense against knives, claws, and teeth.

Every constable carries a hooked crowbill truncheon, a broad constable’s hanger, whistle, alarm-rattle, and restraints. Patrols commonly work in pairs: one constable bears the bull’s-eye lantern while the other carries a heavy six-shot service revolver.

Vigilance armories maintain specialist ammunition made with silver, salt, iron, wood, and other materials. Unfortunately, constables do not always learn what they are hunting before they must shoot it.

Vigilance Houses

The principal headquarters is Central Vigilance Hall, almost universally called the Black Hall. It contains the offices of the Chief Vigilant, the central records archive, interrogation rooms, an extensive armory, evidence vaults, and several levels of cells. Its lowest cells were constructed for prisoners who cannot be safely hanged, drowned, poisoned, or allowed to see the moon.

Each major district maintains a smaller Vigilance House, commonly called a Black House. These fortified station houses contain a public desk, ready room, holding cells, equipment lockers, and a small dead-house. The constables assigned to one Black House are collectively called a Watch.

Small lantern posts and sentry rooms supplement the Black Houses in crowded or strategically important neighborhoods. A citizen may report a crime at any of them, though whether anything is done depends greatly upon the citizen, the crime, and the district.

The Vigilance maintains a fortified station on the edge of the Shambles rather than deep within it. From there, Blackcoats enter the outer districts in groups of six or more. Locals say its great iron doors were designed less to keep prisoners in than to let the constables get back inside quickly.

Patrols

Blackcoats walk established routes called rounds. A standard patrol consists of two constables, while four are assigned to docks, markets, tram stations, and neighborhoods suffering recent disturbances. Six or more enter the Shambles, Gutterkin territory, or any building from which the previous patrol failed to return.

At fixed points along a round, the lantern-bearing constable marks the patrol ledger or reports to a Vigilance post. If a patrol misses two consecutive marks, another patrol is sent to investigate. If that patrol also disappears, the street may simply be closed until morning.

Blackcoats are expected to intervene in:

  • Murder, assault, robbery, kidnapping, and public dueling
  • Riots, gang warfare, and unlawful assemblies
  • Cult activity and forbidden religious rites
  • Unlicensed sorcery or magical disturbances
  • Dangerous creatures inside inhabited districts
  • Unquiet corpses and improperly managed hauntings
  • Damage to civic buildings, tram lines, bridges, and public monuments
  • Violations of quarantine, curfew, or catastrophe restrictions

They generally ignore private gambling, discreet vice, and minor smuggling unless ordered otherwise or denied their customary consideration.

Performing Their Duties

A Blackcoat’s first task is to restore order, not determine innocence. Combatants are separated, weapons confiscated, doors forced open, and anyone still arguing may be struck until the situation becomes easier to understand.

Suspects are bound and taken to the nearest Black House. Witnesses are questioned separately, statements are recorded, and physical evidence is tagged for examination. When magic or monsters are involved, the Watch may summon a licensed magician, surgeon, creature examiner, or specialist Vigilance detail.

Constables possess broad authority to search property during fires, riots, declared hunts, magical emergencies, and outbreaks of unnatural disease. In wealthier districts, this authority is exercised with paperwork and apologies. In poorer districts, the crowbill usually arrives before the warrant.

Blackcoats seldom chase a fleeing suspect blindly into the fog. One constable follows while the other sounds the alarm-rattle, summoning nearby patrols to close streets, alleys, bridges, and tram platforms. Experienced criminals know that the Vigilance does not need to run quickly; it merely needs to know where one sleeps.

Reputation

Respectable citizens describe the Civic Vigilance as stern but necessary. The poor call it an armed collection service. Criminals regard individual Blackcoats as obstacles, customers, or competitors. Monsters tend to fear the lanterns more than the uniforms.

The Vigilance contains brave constables, petty tyrants, exhausted veterans, ambitious investigators, and officers who have become indistinguishable from the criminals they police. Most are united by one hard truth:

Fogport is worse without them.
